clusters.title: Older women are as varied and individual as we have ever been | Letters
clusters.neutral_headline: Older women are as varied and individual as we have ever been | Letters

items.title: Older women are as varied and individual as we have ever been | Letters
items.standfirst: Thank you, Jo Brand, for not offering us a formula for growing older, writes Dr Denise Taylor. Plus a letter from Louise Mothersole I found Jo Brand’s reflections on approaching 70 wonderfully refreshing (‘It’s far too late for me to go to the gym every 10 minutes’: Jo Brand on ageing, raging, fitness and grief, 2 November). Here is a woman who doesn’t feel obliged to turn ageing into another self-improvement project. She can be angry, grumpy, less adventurous than she once was, and still enjoy her life.We hear so much about ageing well, ageing positively and ageing successfully. We are encouraged to exercise more, eat better, remain productive, find our purpose and keep reinventing ourselves. Much of this advice is well intentioned, but collectively it can make growing older seem like another job we are expected to perform. Continue reading...

clusters.title: It is time the government treated hunger and obesity as two interlinked problems | Letter
clusters.neutral_headline: It is time the government treated hunger and obesity as...

items.title: It is time the government treated hunger and obesity as two interlinked problems | Letter
items.standfirst: The cabinet committee the MPs want should become the delivery arm of a statutory right to adequate food, writes Prof Kent Buse of the World Obesity FederationYour report (UK government’s obesity plan ‘doomed to fail’, MPs warn, 30 October) arrives a fortnight after the Right to Food UK Commission asked the same prime minister for the same thing: a legal duty on government, a minister responsible for it, and an independent body reporting to parliament.Each report sees half the problem. The Health and Social Care Committee wants prevention and treatment run as separate workstreams, and stops at urging ministers to stand up to the food industry. The commission sees hunger as a question of income and rights, but says little about the quality of the diet that low incomes buy. The same food system, and the same households, produce both hunger and obesity. Whitehall treats them as two problems, with two sets of ministers and no shared accountability, and so neither is solved. Continue reading...

items.title: Tired all the time? What to know about B12 and if it actually boosts energy levels
items.standfirst: Med spas are raving about vitamin B12 shots as a pick-me-up. But do they actually make you feel more energized?If you spend time on social media, you may have seen med spa owners and employees describing vitamin B12 shots as a pick-me-up. When they’re run down or facing a busy week, they say, a quick injection gets them through. Some med spas say many people feel an energy lift within a day or two and recommend a shot every few weeks.B12 is essential to your health, and people who don’t get enough of it can feel exhausted or worse. But most people already have plenty of B12, and for them, extra doses aren’t likely to help. Continue reading...

clusters.title: ‘I was in a darker place than I’d ever been. ECT was my only hope’: how Ted Scheinman finally broke through his depression
clusters.neutral_headline: ‘I was in a darker place than I’d ever been. ECT was my only hope’: how...

items.title: ‘I was in a darker place than I’d ever been. ECT was my only hope’: how Ted Scheinman finally broke through his depression
items.standfirst: Troubled from the age of three, by 35 the American journalist viewed himself as ‘the lowest piece of dirt on the Earth’ – and neither therapy nor drugs seemed to help. But there was one thing he hadn’t tried …Ted Scheinman can date the origin of his depression with laser accuracy. It was the day he went to the fair, aged three, and returned to his home in upstate New York clutching a Batman toy that he’d won. In the bathroom, he swooped his new doll over the sink. Scheinman had a vivid imagination; in a few years, he would want to become a playwright. To add sound effects and drama, he turned on the tap. There was a whoosh – and the unthinkable happened. Water landed on Batman’s pristine boot in a darkening, enlarging spot that for young Scheinman triggered several rapid thoughts, the last of them being: “I am going to die.”Now 41, Scheinman, a senior editor at Smithsonian magazine, has written a memoir of his “life as a depressive”. Jolt: My Electric Journey Out of Darkness charts his path from toddlerhood to the point in 2020, at the age of 35, when he referred himself for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). By then, he was in “a much darker place” than he had ever been – and regarded himself as “the lowest piece of dirt on the Earth”. The treatment was “not so much a last resort … as my only hope”, he says. Continue reading...

items.title: New drug could be cure for common cause of high blood pressure
items.standfirst: Benefits of baxdrostat are unexpectedly found to remain up to two years after patients stop taking itMillions of people with high blood pressure stand to benefit from a new drug that has stunned doctors by reversing a common cause of the condition for years after patients stopped taking the medication.Patients who took the drug, called baxdrostat, saw their blood pressure improve during a six- to 12-month course of the daily pills, but unexpectedly the benefits remained up to two years later, with some patients no longer on any hypertension drugs and potentially cured of the condition. items.title: ‘What is this emotion telling me?’ How anger, fear and jealousy can point the way to a better life
items.standfirst: It’s tempting to ignore uncomfortable feelings – but maybe they’re the key to a happier, more successful future. Time to increase your psychological flexibility …Something infuriating happened to me recently. My local gym closed down, and overnight what I laughingly call my fitness regime was toast. Quite literally, because now instead of plodding, spinning and lifting tiny dumbbells, I was spending my early mornings guzzling lavishly buttered sourdough.Obviously, I could have brainstormed alternatives, from going for a run outside or taking an online class to – simple plan – joining one of the five other gyms in my neighbourhood. But instead I chose to see the inconvenience of it all. I grew creakier and crankier by the day. Continue reading...

clusters.neutral_headline: New ‘high safety’ chemicals in plastic food packaging linked to...

items.title: New ‘high safety’ chemicals in plastic food packaging linked to lower birth weight, study finds
items.standfirst: Dinch, an allegedly ‘safe’ alternative, used in the EU and US also found to cause fetal development complicationsExposure to a new generation of allegedly “safe” plasticizers is linked to lower birth weight and fetal development complications, which could cause serious health problems later in life, a new peer-reviewed study found.As the health risks in exposure to common phthalate plasticizers became clear over the last few decades, industry began switching to a new type of chemical, called Dinch, that it claimed was a “high safety”, nontoxic alternative. It is widely used in soft plastic food packaging in the United States and European Union, and is found in children’s toys, medical devices, some textiles, flooring and other consumer goods. Continue reading...
